_doc: W. Ross Ashby's journal (The W. Ross Ashby Digital Archive) as a register the system works from. The keyword and category parts are generated by `python3 -m foundation ashbyarchive --build DIR --apply` from pages fetched at the archive's robots.txt crawl delay; principles, systems_categories and not_applicable are written by hand and checked. Principles are stated in our own words with Ashby's page numbers; the journal's text is copyright of the Ashby estate and is not copied here.

principles.statement: Parts adapt at the same time only when a disperser keeps their trials apart; two parts trying changes on one shared step-function at once judge each other's change as their own. One trial per step-function at a time; independent parts still adapt in parallel.

Each change is tested by the whole system, not only by the variable it was made for: making one variable more stable can make the whole unstable, and parts talk to each other through the environment. Every settled action is read against every other essential variable of its scope.
Some step-functions can be used only once, so an adapting system slowly loses versatility. The system measures how many of its step-functions can still move.
Only variety can absorb variety: the second loop needs step-functions it can change and a wide channel from its essential variables to them, or it cannot answer the disturbances it meets.

Improvement comes by trial and the elimination of what fails: a step is kept only if it brings the variable back, undone otherwise, and the search goes on through untried values until a configuration holds. The rate of change is bounded so the search does not destroy what it found.

An adapting system has to get its forgetting right and needs long-term as well as short-term memory: what it tried in one episode is forgotten when the variable is back in bounds, while lessons that hold are kept in code.
probes: grep:foundation/ultrastability.py::episode = \[s for s in steps if s\["n"\] > last_ok\]

principles.statement: Knowing means controlling: a claim about the system counts only when a probe of its behaviour backs it, and a prediction is knowledge only once it is scored against what happened.
A very large system is observed through a few statistics chosen because they are likely to show a runaway, and ultrastability is shown only by disturbing the system on purpose.

A society or organization is a multistable system: its laws are step-functions, its memory is standing orders, its joins should be minimal and target-setting is its control. Standing rules live as code the loops read, and goals carry their own knobs.

An essential variable drives its own repair with noise in proportion to how far it is out of limits: the second loop's search first draws near the current value, within a window that widens with the deviation, and only then over the whole range.
